Each solution starts from the uncompressed object, identifies the bottleneck, and states the invariant that justifies the compressed structure.

# A. K-th Distinct Substring

### How to find it

View distinct substrings as nonempty paths from the SAM root. Count paths in reverse length order, then skip lexicographic transition blocks.

### Correctness

Each distinct substring spells exactly one root path. Each outgoing transition partitions paths by their first next character, so block subtraction selects exactly the k-th path.

### Complexity

`O(n log alphabet)` time and `O(n alphabet)` memory in the fixed-array implementation.

### Reconstruction trace and traps

An outgoing letter block contains the one substring ending after that edge and
all extensions below it, hence size `1+dp[next]`. Iterate letters in order,
subtract entire blocks, append the selected letter, and stop when the remaining
rank is one. Otherwise decrement once and continue below the edge.

Do not multiply by occurrence count in this distinct-substring problem. Cap DP
counts before overflow and report impossibility when `k` exceeds `dp[root]`.

# B. Longest Common Substring

### How to find it

Build a SAM for the first string and maintain the longest suffix of each scanned prefix of the second string that the automaton accepts.

### Correctness

The scan invariant gives the longest common substring ending at every position of the second string. Taking the maximum therefore considers every possible endpoint.

### Complexity

`O(|a|+|b|)` time and `O(|a| alphabet)` memory.

### State repair and tests

On a missing edge, follow suffix links until an edge exists or the root is
reached. After a retreat, set the current matched length to at most the new
state's `len`; then consume the character. The maximum over all scanned
positions considers every possible endpoint in the second string.

Test no common character, complete containment, repeated borders, and a match
that survives several suffix-link retreats. Resetting length to zero after
every missing transition loses valid shorter suffix matches.

# C. Palindrome Prefix Profile

### How to find it

A newly appended character can introduce only one new distinct palindrome: the longest palindromic suffix. Maintain it with palindromic suffix links.

### Correctness

Every new occurrence ends at the appended position. Shorter palindromic suffixes already occurred as suffixes of the previous longest one; creation of exactly the missing longest node is therefore necessary and sufficient.

### Complexity

`O(n alphabet)` stored transitions and amortized `O(n)` traversal.

### Creation invariant and tests

After appending at position `i`, follow links until the characters surrounding
the candidate suffix agree. If its transition already exists, no distinct node
is created. Otherwise create the new longest palindromic suffix and find its
proper palindromic suffix link with the same search from the parent's link.

The `-1` and `0` roots must never be counted as text palindromes. Test one
character, even palindromes, nested odd palindromes, and repeated occurrences
that must reuse an existing node.

# D. Shortest Absent Word

### How to find it

A word is a substring exactly when it labels a SAM root path. Breadth-first search those paths in letter order and stop at the first missing transition.

### Correctness

BFS processes path labels by increasing length and, within a level, lexicographic order. A missing next edge certifies absence, so the first such label meets both tie-breaks.

### Complexity

`O(n alphabet)` time and memory.

### BFS order and correctness details

Queue accepted SAM paths, not arbitrary state visits: different path labels
can end in the same state but are different candidate words. Process outgoing
letters in sorted order. The first absent transition encountered is shortest
because of BFS depth and lexicographically smallest because parents and edges
are expanded in lexicographic level order.

Marking states as visited is wrong here—it collapses distinct words sharing an
end-position class. Tests should include a missing one-letter word, an alphabet
whose every letter occurs, and several shortest absent words with a tie.
